description: Just another team floating through the universe.
summary:
Maia is a health-monitoring software for astronauts that helps them look out for their own health while in spacial missions where they need to recognize changes in their own bodies and take action about them. 
The idea of this project is to use the data given by biometric sensors in the spacesuits to learn each astronaut’s own baseline in different indicators of health as such as heart rate, core temperature, blood pressure, etc. Also keeping track of each measurement along the mission and compare it with the baseline to look for possible health affections on each person based in their own flags, and based on these analysis results, we don’t look for a diagnosis, but an explanation for the astronaut to understand what is going on with themselves, what can they do about it and how to do it during different situations such as EVA's (Extravehicular Activities) or inside the ship.
details:
Maia is health-monitoring software that helps astronauts who are not doctors understand their own data and gives their flight surgeon an analysis they can act on. Its central idea is to compare each astronaut’s measurements with their own baseline, show how much evidence supports a change, and offer a clear next step. The interface brings together a body map, simulated vital signs, guided measurements, symptom logging, mission context, and emergency button.

Maia is designed to support decisions; it does not diagnose.

During a long mission, the crew may need to decide what to do before they can reach someone on Earth. A single blood pressure reading, for example, may be hard to interpret on its own. Maia shows that reading alongside the astronaut’s usual range and recent measurements. For daily trends, it looks for at least four of the last six days outside the personal range in the same direction. It also shows when readings are missing or out of date so the crew can judge how much information they have. Occasional lab tests are handled separately and compared with the astronaut’s own preflight results.

The location selector in the top bar lets the crew switch between On the ISS, Spacewalk, and Back on Earth. On the ISS, the crew can use the daily monitoring tools and review environmental information such as cabin CO₂, radiation, space weather, and the station’s position. Spacewalk opens a suit check before the astronaut goes out. Once the simulated spacewalk begins, the visor displays suit pressure, suit CO₂, heart rate, and time remaining. The astronaut can have the readings read aloud and log a note. Back on Earth focuses on readaptation after landing, with information such as standing blood pressure, heart rate, and sleep. Lunar Surface and Mars Transit can also be selected as previews. They show how factors such as gravity, radiation, and communication delay would change the monitoring context.

The Emergency section starts with what the crew can observe and leads to a guide where they can check off actions and document what happened. The Reports section then brings together health changes, readings, symptoms, mission events, and crew notes. The astronaut gets a plain-language summary and can preview the more detailed view prepared for the flight surgeon. For example, a crew member who logs headaches can review when they occurred alongside sleep records and cabin CO₂ readings. Seeing them on the same timeline helps the astronaut describe what happened and gives the medical team information to investigate.

We got creative with how the crew moves through the information. The home screen is laid out like an orbit, with a small asteroid mascot at the center that gives reminders about habits such as drinking water, resting, and exercising. The body map turns a list of measurements into something the crew can explore by selecting the area they’re concerned about. The visor changes the interface to suit a different task, keeping the readings needed during a spacewalk in view. We wanted those design choices to make Maia easier to use in a real situation, especially when the astronaut has little time to look through menus.

As a team, we considered communication delays, limited bandwidth, differences between astronauts, the quality of the available data, and how easy the interface would be to use under pressure as well as in missions. We paired status colors with words and icons, offered spoken readings, and made it clear when environmental information comes from a saved copy. We added illustrated instructions that guide astronauts through each test step by step, along with hands-on, interactive checks they can complete directly in the app, such as the vision and attention tests.

We built the web app with React, TypeScript, and Vite, used three.js for the mascot, and developed the backend with Python and FastAPI. For the analysis, we used Python, pandas, NumPy, and SciPy to process public Inspiration4 lab results from NASA’s Open Science Data Repository. NASA DONKI and NOAA provide data about the space environment. The prototype runs in a browser, uses the device’s camera and speech features, and demonstrates wearable sensor readings with labeled simulations.

Our expected impact is to help astronauts notice changes in their health, take a clearer next step on board, and share information their flight surgeon can review more easily. Connecting real sensors and testing Maia with crew members in realistic mission scenarios would help us see how well the design works in practice.
